articles.summary: Former Amb. Gordon Sondland's "Godfather Test" urges NATO and the European Union to presume Vladimir Putin is behind cyberattacks and sabotage targeting the West.
articles.body: In one of the most memorable scenes in "The Godfather," Don Vito Corleone gathers the heads of New York’s crime families to make peace and secure the return of his son Michael. "But I’m a superstitious man," he tells them. He warns that if Michael should suffer some supposedly random misfortune—an implausible suicide, a fatal accident or even a bolt of lightning—"then I’m going to blame some of the people in this room…" RUSSIA PREPARING HYBRID ATTACKS ON NATO'S EASTERN FLANK, INTELLIGENCE WARNS The message was unmistakable: Do not hide an attack behind coincidence, an intermediary or a carefully manufactured lack of proof. Whatever disguise is chosen, I will know where it came from, and I will hold the responsible people accountable. It is time for NATO and the European Union to adopt what might be called the Godfather Test. If a drone mysteriously crosses into the territory of an Eastern European country, we should presume Vladimir Putin is responsible. If a power cable is severed beneath the Baltic Sea, we should presume Vladimir Putin is responsible. US INTEL WARNS RUSSIA COULD LAUNCH LIMITED ATTACK ON NATO ALLY IN EFFORT TO FRAGMENT ORGANIZATION: REPORT If a government network is crippled, a weapons factory explodes, a railway system is disrupted or a political figure suddenly becomes the beneficiary of a sophisticated disinformation campaign, we should presume Vladimir Putin is responsible. Putin can then prove that he was not. This reverses the way the West has traditionally approached such events. Our democracies are built upon the presumption of innocence. It is one of our most important values, and it must remain inviolate when we administer justice to individuals through our courts. But Vladimir Putin is not a defendant standing in an American courtroom. Russia is not entitled to the protections of the Bill of Rights, a jury of its peers or an endless international discovery process before the West acts to defend itself. We have no obligation to presume that the Kremlin is innocent while it is accorded some imaginary form of geopolitical due process. Yet that is effectively what we have been doing. Russia exploits our own system of innocence until guilt is proven, turning one of democracy’s greatest virtues into a strategic vulnerability. I’M PRESIDENT OF ONE OF AMERICA’S MOST RELIABLE ALLIES. HERE’S HOW WE STAND UP TO RUSSIA The Kremlin understands that Western governments are reluctant to act without evidence that can be publicly disclosed and defended beyond a reasonable doubt. So Russia structures its operations to ensure that such evidence will rarely exist—or cannot be revealed without compromising intelligence sources and methods. Putin forfeited the benefit of the doubt long ago. He forfeited it through the invasion of neighboring countries, the use of proxies and cutouts, cyberattacks, political interference, assassinations, sabotage, energy coercion and an endless stream of denials that collapses under scrutiny only after the damage is done. A government that repeatedly commits arson should not be treated as an innocent bystander every time smoke rises from another building. GERMANY BLAMES RUSSIA AFTER EXPLOSIVE-LADEN DRONE FOUND NEAR UKRAINIAN CARGO PLANES AT MAJOR AIRPORT For years, Russia has operated inside the gray zone between peace and open warfare. Its actions are designed to be damaging enough to weaken its adversaries but sufficiently murky to prevent a decisive response. Moscow uses anonymous hackers, commercial vessels, intelligence operatives, fabricated local movements and supposedly independent criminal organizations. It obscures responsibility, demands impossible standards of proof and then ridicules the West for its uncertainty. The tactic works because we allow it to work. When suspicious acts of sabotage or destabilization threaten NATO or EU countries and bear the hallmarks of Russian activity, Moscow should be treated as responsible unless persuasive evidence demonstrates otherwise. Every incident is treated as an entirely new mystery. Governments open investigations, consult experts, compare intelligence and debate attribution. Months pass. The public loses interest. Allies disagree over whether the evidence clears some arbitrary threshold. Russia denies everything, and the matter quietly disappears. By then, the Kremlin has already moved on to its next operation. NATO ALLY POLAND WARNS RUSSIA, BELARUS PUSHING ILLEGAL MIGRANTS TOWARD ALLIANCE — AND THE US Our excessive caution does not make us judicious. It makes us predictable. Putin knows that unless he launches a conventional attack with Russian flags flying from every tank, NATO will argue with itself over whether he was really responsible. That hesitation is not an unfortunate side effect of his strategy. It is the central objective. The West must reverse both the presumption and the incentive. When suspicious acts of sabotage or destabilization threaten NATO or EU countries and bear the hallmarks of Russian activity, Moscow should be treated as responsible unless persuasive evidence demonstrates otherwise. REPORT WARNS RUSSIA USING SHADOW FLEET TO PROBE NATO DRONE DEFENSES And each event should be met with an asymmetric ratcheting up of the costs imposed on Russia. If the Kremlin damages a cable, we need not damage a Russian cable. If it attacks a government computer network, we need not attack an identical network in return. Symmetrical retaliation allows Putin to calculate the price in advance and treat it as merely another cost of doing business. Our response should instead occur in an area Putin values, at a time of our choosing and at a cost greater than the benefit Russia obtained from its original attack. TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT? That might mean quietly disabling a Russian military capability, compromising an intelligence network, obstructing a revenue stream, exposing hidden assets, disrupting sanctions evasion or increasing the effectiveness of Ukrainian operations. The precise response should depend upon the circumstances, but the governing formula must be simple: every act of Russian mischief leaves the Kremlin worse off than it was before. Nor should we feel compelled to announce what we have done. RUSSIA THREATENS STRIKES ON UK MILITARY TARGETS, ‘CATASTROPHIC CONSEQUENCES’ OVER UKRAINE Russia does not hold a press conference after every cyberattack, act of sabotage or covert operation. Neither should we. There is no strategic virtue in providing Putin with a detailed accounting of our capabilities, methods and decision-making. We should be as quiet about our response as Russia is about its attack. Putin should know that a price has been paid, but he need not always know precisely when, where or how it was imposed. Uncertainty has been one of his most effective weapons. It is time for the West to use uncertainty as well. NATO'S EASTERN FLANK RACES TO REARM AS TRUMP PRESSURE EXPOSES WESTERN EUROPE'S DEFENSE GAP This does not mean responding impulsively to every electrical failure, industrial accident or unexplained drone. Intelligence still matters. Judgment still matters. Allied coordination still matters. The presumption should be strong, not mindless. But we must stop requiring courtroom-grade proof before defending countries and institutions that are not courtrooms. National security decisions have always been made using intelligence assessments, patterns of conduct, capabilities, motives and probabilities. Absolute certainty is rarely available—and insisting upon it simply gives the aggressor a veto over our response. Some will object that this creates a risk of miscalculation. Of course, it does. But our present policy creates a much larger risk: that Putin will continue escalating because he believes the West is institutionally incapable of responding to anything short of a full-scale invasion. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Deterrence is not achieved by proving responsibility to a mathematical certainty months after every attack. It is achieved by convincing an adversary beforehand that his actions will carry consequences. Europe has spent decades constructing elaborate legal and diplomatic processes while Putin has spent those same decades learning how to manipulate them. He understands that democratic governments fear acting on incomplete information. He therefore ensures that the information will always be incomplete. We should stop rewarding him for his craftsmanship. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The presumption should now be simple. If serious misfortune befalls one of the countries in Putin’s sights—through a drone, a cyberattack, a mysterious explosion, a damaged pipeline or some other extraordinarily convenient accident—we are going to blame the man in the room who has repeatedly threatened us, attacked his neighbors and perfected the art of deniable aggression. Then we will respond asymmetrically, quietly and with enough force to ensure that the next act of mischief costs him even more—even if we fail to meet the "beyond a reasonable doubt" hurdle. articles.title: In 1888, Wisconsin publisher and women’s-rights pioneer Lisle Lester died penniless in New York; her ashes went unclaimed for 138 years and are finally returning home to Fond du Lac
articles.summary: US News: For 138 years, the remains of Lisle Lester, a Fond du Lac woman who became known as a journalist, publisher, actress and advocate for women’s rights, .
articles.body: For 138 years, the remains of Lisle Lester, a Fond du Lac woman who became known as a journalist, publisher, actress and advocate for women’s rights, remained unclaimed in a New York mortuary. Now, after years of efforts by women in her former Wisconsin community, Lester is finally coming home.Lester was born Sophia Walker in 1837 and moved to Fond du Lac when she was six years old, NBC 6 reported. She later built a career that took her far beyond Wisconsin, becoming known for her work in publishing and on stage, as well as for supporting causes she believed in.“She wore many hats,” said Tracy Reinhardt, a local historian and historical consultant for the Fond du Lac Soroptimist Education Committee. Reinhardt also described Lester as a major but little-known figure from the city's past.Lester started The Badger State Monthly in 1859, which is described as the first magazine published in Wisconsin. Her work also helped women enter the printing industry. She trained women to work as typesetters at a time when the field was largely dominated by men.Publisher who challenged normsLester's work in publishing was not easy. According to Reinhardt, men did not want her admitted to the Wisconsin editorial group of the time, forcing her to fight for a place in the industry.Her writing also attracted criticism. Fellow writer Mark Twain once called her “the worst writer in the world”. Reinhardt said Twain believed that if Lester wrote a 100-word paragraph, he could express the same idea in 20 words.But the criticism did not stop Lester from continuing her work. “Public opinion, I don't think meant or had an impact on her,” Reinhardt said as quoted by NBC 26. “She still did her thing.”Lester also had a career in theatre and travelled across the United States and other countries for her performances. Her audiences included prominent political and royal figures.“She went to countries like Japan, China... she was a guest in the palace of the kings and the queens that were ruling those countries at the time,” Reinhardt said.Her public life was not limited to publishing and acting. Lester also used her position to support causes she cared about, including women's rights and other social issues.“You couldn't pigeonhole her to being an abolitionist or women's suffragette or anything like that because she embraced all issues,” Reinhardt said.From wealth to dying pennilessDespite earning substantial money through her acting career, Lester eventually died without money. Reinhardt said Lester would sometimes stop performing when she became interested in a cause and devote herself to it instead.“Unfortunately, when she would find a cause that she was interested in, she would just stop her performances and take on these causes,” Reinhardt said. “She lived off her savings, and eventually drained it dry the last 10 years of her life.”Lester died in New York in 1888 at the age of 50. She was cremated, but her remains were never claimed by family. They remained in a New York mortuary for more than a century.Her story came back into focus in Fond du Lac in 2024, when the Soroptimist International of Fond du Lac learned more about her and began working to bring her remains back to Wisconsin.The effort was taken up by several women in the community, including Reinhardt and Dawn Nelson, director of Zacherl Funeral Home. Nelson said she became involved because she believed Lester deserved to be properly laid to rest.“I'm very passionate about people being laid to rest properly,” Nelson said. “Knowing that a woman died in poverty after trying so hard to advocate for women and women's rights, and died alone and poor is just really sad.”Years of work to bring her homeGetting Lester's remains back to Wisconsin involved more than simply arranging transportation. The effort included red tape, court hearings and fees.Nelson said the New York mortuary initially wanted almost $8,000 to return the remains. That amount was beyond what the group could afford, so she continued looking for a way to reduce the cost.“The third time that I called, I actually asked to speak to a female funeral director,” Nelson said. “Not kidding!”After asking questions and working through the arrangements, Nelson was able to reduce the cost to $3,000. At the time of the 2024 report, the group had raised about one-third of that amount and hoped to collect the rest.The effort eventually succeeded. The Fond du Lac Soroptimists received Lester's remains on Friday, September 4, 2026, ending a wait that had lasted 138 years, according to AOL.Lester's return will now allow her to be buried in the community where she spent her early years and began her remarkable career. Her burial service is scheduled for 10 am on October 17 at Calvary Cemetery in Fond du Lac.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: America's biggest beer-loving states revealed — see where yours ranks
articles.summary: America's beer capital runs through Wisconsin for the second straight year, with the Midwest dubbed the nation's "beer belt." Regional loyalty remains strong, experts say.
articles.body: Beer has a storied history in the United States and was a common beverage in colonial America. Its influence on the nation's culture remains strong – and a new study found which states appear to be most interested in beer. "Wisconsin is still America's beer capital," reported consumer research firm Innerbody Research in the website's recently released analysis of a year's worth of Google Trends search data. This marks the second year in a row the Badger State came out on top in the rankings. Innerbody labeled the Midwest "America's beer belt," since "Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, North Dakota, South Dakota and Missouri all rank among the nation's top 10," and "every Midwestern state finishes in the top 20." GEORGE WASHINGTON'S 1757 BEER RECIPE BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE AHEAD OF AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY "The Midwest is one of many regions with a deep historic beer culture tied to both a long legacy of regional production and reinvigorated by craft brewers in recent decades," Bart Watson, president and CEO of the Colorado-based Brewers Association, told Fox News Digital. Wyoming came in second place for its search-interest score. Kansas, Nebraska and Iowa came in third, fourth and fifth, respectively. States along the Pacific coast showed lower beer-related search interest, according to the study. Alaska, Washington, California, Oregon and Hawaii were in the bottom 10 for beer searches. When it comes to specific brands, regional loyalty remains strong. "The local dominance of a beer brand is almost entirely driven by historic entry advantage," Jean-Pierre H. Dubé, a marketing professor at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, who has published research explaining the regional dominance of brands, told Fox News Digital. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Miller dominates in Wisconsin because it was first to market there. In contrast, Budweiser was first to market in St. Louis, where it also remains dominant. The prevalence of beer tastes in the Midwest reflects the fact that most of the world's largest brewers in the late 1800s were in the Midwest in St. Louis, Wisconsin and Chicago – but especially Wisconsin." Samuel Adams "launched in Boston and was arguably the first successful craft brewer to become a dominant brand and obtain national distribution," Dubé added. Michelob Ultra generated the most search interest among the beer brands analyzed and also came out on top in Alabama, Nevada and Oklahoma. "One of beer's strengths is the many options for lower calories and ABV relative to other adult beverages," Watson said. "Light beers underline that quality and have been very popular ever since they were introduced. In recent years, interest in particular attributes, like low-carb beers, has also been a factor in consumer preferences." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Stella Artois was the most popular beer in Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Louisiana, New York, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Virginia and Washington, D.C. Along with other imported beers, Stella is "perceived as a premium beer in the U.S.," though that isn't its reputation in the brand's home market of Belgium, Dubé said. Dubé's studies have found that exposure to certain beers when consumers first reach legal drinking age influences what they prefer later in life. "Millennials in cities with few craft brands at 21 drink way more national-brand beer today – Bud and Miller – than millennials in cities with relatively more craft beer brands when they came of age," he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Beer Marketer Insights reported this year that Michelob Ultra had overtaken Bud Light and Modelo Especial to become the top-selling beer in the U.S. by volume. Sales and search aren't perfectly correlated, Watson said, and the Innerbody findings "signal something about new interest and brands as much as overall brand strength or sales." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "A sales map would undoubtedly look very different," he said. "At the end of the day, beer is supposed to be fun, so no one should take them too seriously, and they are best argued over with friends and family with a beer in hand."

articles.title: Fuel duty proposal withdrawn in Jersey after discussions
articles.summary: Deputy Lucy Stephenson had wanted to cut the tax by 10p a litre for three months.
articles.body:
A bid to reduce fuel duty for three months to help motorists deal with the cost of living crisis has been withdrawn.

Deputy Lucy Stephenson put forward her proposition to Jersey's States Assembly in June which called for the tax - currently around the 65p per litre mark - added to petrol and diesel prices to be cut by 10p a litre from 1 October to 31 December.

However, Stephenson said she had withdrawn the proposal following "constructive discussions" with Treasury Minister Alan Maclean.

She said the talks had produced a "pragmatic way forward" to help islanders deal with financial issues.

When Stephenson lodged her proposition in June , the St Mary, St Ouen and St Peter deputy said the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, which led to limited traffic moving through the Strait of Hormuz , had exacerbated "spiralling costs" for Jersey residents.

She said her discussions with Maclean and other colleagues at the States had left her satisfied the issue was being taken seriously.

"I think there were very clear messages at the recent election from voters about the cost of living," Stephenson said.

"It's obvious people are struggling and we have heard that loud and clear."

The budget is due to be lodged by the government later in September before being debated by the States in December.

articles.title: What does the law say about inheritance? Know your rights
articles.summary: India News: For generations, inheritance in India has been shaped by family relationships, religious personal laws and the nature of the property being inherited..
articles.body: For generations, inheritance in India has been shaped by family relationships, religious personal laws and the nature of the property being inherited.A daughter may have an equal right with her brother in one situation, but not necessarily in another. A widow may be entitled to a share in her husband's estate, while a woman may also own property in her own right through inheritance, gifts or other means.The biggest question often arises when a person dies without leaving a will. In such cases, known as intestate succession, the applicable law determines who inherits and in what proportion. The rules differ across religious communities.The Hindu Succession Act, 1956, governs succession among Hindus and also applies to Buddhists, Jains and Sikhs, subject to its provisions. Muslims are generally governed by Muslim personal law on intestate succession, while Christians and Parsis are principally covered by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.So what can a woman legally claim?Hindu women: Daughter has equal coparcenary rightsOne of the biggest changes in women's inheritance rights came with the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, which made a daughter a coparcener by birth in a Hindu joint family governed by Mitakshara law, with the same rights and liabilities as a son.The Supreme Court's 2020 judgment in Vineeta Sharma v Rakesh Sharma clarified that this right is by birth and does not depend on the father being alive when the 2005 amendment came into force.Marriage also does not take away a daughter's coparcenary rights.But an important distinction must be made between coparcenary property and a parent's self-acquired property.If a Hindu father dies intestate leaving behind his wife, son and daughter and the property is his self-acquired property, all children and the widow are Class I heirs. In a simple example involving Rs 1 crore, the wife, son and daughter would each receive about Rs 33.33 lakh.Advocate Rupali Jain explains why the calculation can be very different for coparcenary property. If the Rs 1 crore is Mitakshara coparcenary property, the father's notional share is first calculated. His share is then distributed among the relevant Class I heirs.On that calculation, Jain says, "wife receives about Rs 11.11 lakh and each child Rs 44.44 lakh."The example highlights an important point: a daughter is not automatically entitled to "half" the property simply because she is a daughter. The nature of the property must first be established.Another common misconception is that every property owned by a parent is ancestral property in which children have a birthright. That is not necessarily so.Muslim women: Share depends on the family structureMuslim inheritance in India operates under Muslim personal law, which does not follow the same joint-family property model.Islamic inheritance rules identify different categories of heirs and prescribe shares depending on which relatives survive the deceased. The applicable school of Muslim law can also matter.The daughter will generally receive half the son's share but the actual calculation depends on all the surviving heirs.A widow's share also depends on whether the deceased leaves descendants. Broadly, under commonly applied Sunni rules, a widow receives one-eighth where there are children or certain descendants and one-fourth where there are none."The share of a Muslim woman therefore has to be calculated based on the complete family structure," said advocate Pritish Sunil Teckchandani.Muslim testamentary succession is also different. Generally, a Muslim's power to make a will is restricted to one-third of the estate without the consent of the heirs, subject to applicable personal-law rules.Christian women: Sons and daughters inherit equallyFor Christians, intestate succession is primarily governed by the Indian Succession Act, 1925.Where a Christian man dies without a will leaving a widow and children, the widow receives one-third of the estate, while the remaining two-thirds goes equally to the children.For example, if a Christian man dies leaving a wife, one son and one daughter and an estate worth Rs 90 lakh, each would ordinarily receive Rs 30 lakh. "The widow and each child would ordinarily receive one-third each," said Teckchandani.The position changes depending on which relatives survive the deceased, but there is no distinction between sons and daughters in the straightforward situation described above.Unlike Hindu law, Christian succession has no equivalent concept of coparcenary rights by birth. A Christian daughter does not become a co-owner of her father's property merely because she is his daughter; her inheritance generally arises upon succession.Parsi women: Daughter does not lose out to sonParsi intestate succession is governed by special provisions in Part V of the Indian Succession Act. The exact entitlement depends on the relatives who survive the deceased.Thus, where a Parsi man dies intestate leaving a widow, son and daughter, the son and daughter inherit on an equal footing under the applicable rules.The calculation can change where there are more children, a predeceased child, grandchildren or other specified relatives.What happens when there is no willWhen a person dies without a valid will, the property does not automatically go to the eldest son or the closest male relative. The applicable succession law determines who inherits.For Hindus, the Hindu Succession Act lays down a hierarchy of heirs. A widow, son, daughter and mother are among the Class I heirs of a Hindu man who dies intestate.For Muslims, inheritance is calculated under applicable Muslim personal-law rules rather than a Class I heir system.For Christians and Parsis, the relevant provisions of the Indian Succession Act apply.This is why there is no single formula for a woman's inheritance in India. Her share can depend on her religion, relationship to the deceased, the relatives who survive, the nature of the property and whether there is a valid will.What if there is a will — but the daughter gets nothing“For self-acquired property, a Hindu father can generally leave the entire property to his son and exclude his daughter through a valid Will. A daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter,” said Tekchandani.This is where the nature of the property becomes particularly important.A person can generally make a will determining how property that they legally own and can dispose of should be distributed. Therefore, a Hindu father can ordinarily leave his entire self-acquired property to his son and exclude his daughter."The daughter has no compulsory share in such property merely by virtue of being his daughter," said Teckchandani.But a will cannot simply wipe out another person's existing coparcenary interest. A daughter who already has a coparceny share cannot be deprived of that existing interest merely through her father's will."An unfair will is not necessarily an invalid will," explained Teckchandani. However, a woman can challenge a will if there are grounds to question its validity. These can include forgery, lack of testamentary capacity, coercion, undue influence, improper execution or other suspicious circumstances.Jain said courts may examine factors such as whether the testator was elderly, ill or dependent on the beneficiary, whether the beneficiary isolated the testator from other family members, whether there was a sudden departure from an earlier will, or whether the beneficiary was involved in preparing or executing the document."The person alleging coercion must produce credible evidence; mere suspicion or the fact that one child received substantially more property is generally insufficient," said Jain.Medical records, previous wills, messages, bank documents and testimony from doctors, neighbours, lawyers and attesting witnesses may become important evidence.How can one challenge an unfair willThe first step is to establish what the will says and what property it covers.A woman challenging a will should obtain the will, death certificate and relevant property documents. If probate or letters of administration proceedings are pending, she can enter the proceedings and raise objections."If probate proceedings are filed, enter appearance/file objections or a caveat, after which the proceeding becomes contentious," explained Jain.If no such proceedings are pending, the appropriate civil remedy will depend on the circumstances.The court can examine whether the will was properly executed and attested, whether the deceased had testamentary capacity and whether there was fraud, coercion, undue influence or another circumstance affecting its validity.What if a woman is denied her share in propertyThe first step is to establish the property's ownership and character. Sale deeds, title documents, mutation records, partition deeds, gift or settlement deeds, wills and other records can help determine what a woman is actually entitled to.Depending on the dispute, a woman may approach a civil court seeking remedies such as partition and separate possession, declaration of rights, cancellation of an invalid document or an injunction.One of the biggest risks comes when family members ask a daughter to sign a release deed, relinquishment deed, family settlement, partition document or NOC without fully understanding its consequences."The biggest mistake is giving up legal rights informally in the name of maintaining family relations, without understanding the property's character or documenting the settlement," said Jain.A woman should determine whether the property is self-acquired, inherited or coparcenary, establish her legal share and obtain independent advice before signing away any interest.What if the family says she has already given up her shareA daughter may be told that she has no claim because she is married, that her brother "needs the property", or that her share was already given to her through wedding expenses or stridhan.Whether a woman has actually relinquished a property right depends on the applicable law and whether there is a legally valid document or transaction establishing that relinquishment."Family pressure can make people sign documents simply to avoid conflict, but such documents can have significant and sometimes irreversible consequences," said Teckchandani. A verbal family understanding and a legally valid relinquishment or settlement document are not necessarily the same thing.So, what is a woman’s share in family propertyWell, there is no single answer to this question.For a Hindu woman, a daughter can have equal coparcenary rights with a son, while inheritance of self-acquired property after an intestate death follows a different calculation.For a Muslim woman, the share depends on the applicable personal law and the complete family structure. For Christian and Parsi women, succession is principally governed by the Indian Succession Act, with sons and daughters generally treated equally in the relevant intestate situations.A will can also change the outcome, particularly when it concerns property that the testator was free to dispose of. But a will that is unequal is not automatically invalid, nor can it simply extinguish an existing legal interest such as a coparcenary share.For women facing an inheritance dispute, the key questions are therefore: What personal law applies? Who survived the deceased? What kind of property is involved? Was there a valid will? Was the property already transferred or partitioned? And has the woman actually and legally relinquished her share?Knowing the answers to those questions is often the difference between walking away from property and successfully asserting a legal claim.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Prince of Wales to represent King Charles at funeral of King Harald V in Norway
articles.summary: UK News: Prince William will represent King Charles at the funeral of King Harald V in Norway, highlighting royal connections and tributes to the late king.
articles.body: The Prince of Wales, Prince William, will travel to Norway next week to represent his father, King Charles, at the funeral of King Harald V, Buckingham Palace has announced.William will attend the service at Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday alongside his aunt, Princess Anne, who will be there in a private capacity as the godmother of Norway’s new king, Haakon VIII.King Harald died on August 28 aged 89, bringing an end to a 35-year reign in which he became known for his informal approach and close connection with the Norwegian public. Queen Sonja, his widow, is expected to attend the funeral.The King’s decision not to attend follows longstanding royal protocol in which reigning monarchs generally do not attend the funerals of fellow heads of state. William has previously taken on similar duties on his father’s behalf, including representing Charles at the funeral of Pope Francis at the Vatican last April.Charles paid tribute to Harald after his death, remembering his “unwavering dedication” and describing his “kindness, compassion and deep sense of duty”.The British and Norwegian royal families also share a long-standing family connection. Queen Elizabeth II and Harald were second cousins, with both descended from King Edward VII and Queen Alexandra.William and Catherine, Princess of Wales, met Harald and Queen Sonja during their official visit to Norway in 2018. The couple were hosted at the Royal Palace for a banquet, where Harald described them as “family” and praised their support for Queen Elizabeth II.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Algeria civil defence recovers body of 10-year-old boy from well
articles.summary: Child found dead after four-day rescue effort in Algeria’s western province of el-Bayadh.
articles.body:
The body of a 10-year-old boy has been recovered from a well in Algeria’s western province of el-Bayadh, the country’s civil protection agency said, ending a four-day rescue operation that had drawn national attention.

The agency said in a statement on Facebook on Saturday that rescue teams reached the boy, Ayoub, who had died, and recovered his body. It said local authorities and other agencies had mobilised all available resources for the operation.

Ayoub fell into the dry well on Wednesday while walking home in the village of Errokn, in the municipality of Ghassoul. He stepped on a wooden board covering the well opening, which gave way beneath him, and he plunged into the shaft, which was about 80 metres (262 feet) deep and 40cm (15.75 inches) in diameter.

Rescuers were unable to descend into the well, so they dug a parallel shaft to reach the boy through a horizontal passage, using machinery alongside technical experts, work that continued over several days. Loose soil and hard rock layers complicated the effort, officials said.

Authorities in el-Bayadh formed a crisis response unit under the provincial governor, Noureddine Belarbi, involving civil protection, security and military personnel.

Large crowds of residents gathered near the site over the following days to follow the operation and offer support to the family, while additional civil protection units were deployed as the rescue entered what officials described as a “decisive” phase on its fourth day.

Ayoub’s death has revived public debate in Algeria over the safety of unsecured wells in rural areas, with commentators questioning the lack of regulation covering such structures, particularly in isolated regions.

The case recalled the 2018 death of a young man who fell into a 100-metre (328-foot) well in Msila province, where a rescue operation lasted nine days before his body was recovered, and the widely followed 2022 case of Moroccan toddler Rayan, who died after falling into a 32-metre (105-foot) well and being trapped for more than 100 hours in an operation that drew global attention before he was pulled out and later confirmed dead.

articles.body: For nearly two decades, George Lucas pursued a museum that existed first as an idea and then as an increasingly ambitious architectural dream. The filmmaker behind Star Wars and Indiana Jones faced rejected plans, changing locations and years of bureaucracy before the project finally took shape in Los Angeles. Now, after 17 years of setbacks, his $1 billion Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is preparing to open at Exposition Park on September 22, 2026. Designed by architect Ma Yansong and his firm MAD, the futuristic building rises above an 11-acre public park and has already attracted comparisons to a spaceship and a cloud. Inside, visitors will find a vast collection devoted to storytelling through art, illustration, comics and film. For Lucas, the museum represents far more than another cultural institution, it is the realisation of a project he once feared might never happen.George Lucas spent 17 years trying to make the museum happenThe journey began long before the striking Los Angeles building appeared on the horizon. Lucas and his wife, Mellody Hobson, initially explored locations in Chicago and San Francisco, but neither plan ultimately became the home of the museum. Speaking at a press preview, Lucas described the process as a 17-year struggle involving rejected plans, different cities and years spent getting the final building constructed. As reported by Los Angeles Times, Lucas said the experience had involved “17 years between getting kicked out of cities” and trying to make the project happen. He acknowledged that the process nearly broke his determination, despite his reputation for taking on seemingly impossible projects. Eventually, Exposition Park in Los Angeles became the chosen location, giving the museum a permanent home.The $1 billion museum looks like a spaceshipThe building itself may be almost as recognisable as the collection it houses. Designed by Chinese architect Ma Yansong and his firm MAD, the Lucas Museum has an enormous, flowing form that appears to hover above its surroundings. Its unusual silhouette has led many people to compare it with a spaceship, an especially fitting description for a museum founded by the creator of Star Wars. Yansong, however, has also heard the structure compared with a cloud, and welcomed both interpretations. His intention was to create a building that would make people curious before they even entered it. The museum occupies 300,000 square feet, including around 100,000 square feet of gallery space. Its wider campus includes 11 acres of public parkland, an amphitheatre, seating areas and a large fountain called “The Rain”, which also helps cool the building.Inside are 35 galleries devoted to storytellingLucas did not set out to create a conventional museum focused only on traditional fine art. Instead, the institution centres on narrative art, visual works that communicate stories, characters, myths and ideas. Its 35 galleries are arranged around themes including adventure, motherhood, community, childhood illustration, manga and comics. The collection also includes dedicated spaces for artists such as Norman Rockwell, N.C. Wyeth, Frank Frazetta and Maxfield Parrish, alongside a gallery devoted to murals. Lucas has personally shaped the collection over the years, with Hobson saying he effectively dreamed up the museum “from the outside in” and curated it piece by piece. The filmmaker has said one of his strongest motivations was to honour illustrators whose images can give visual form to stories and myths.The Lucas Museum finally opens in Los AngelesThe long wait is now approaching its final chapter. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is scheduled to open to the public on September 22, 2026, after years of construction and planning. Interest has already been building, with visitors reportedly gathering around the site during the summer to catch glimpses of the unusual structure and secure opening-day tickets. The museum is designed to be more than a collection of galleries. Its public park, amphitheatre, fountain, library, café and rooftop Skywalker Grill are intended to make the institution part of everyday life in Los Angeles. For Lucas and Hobson, that accessibility is central to the project's identity. Hobson describes it as a museum “by the people, for the people”, while Lucas frames it as a home for “the people’s art”. After 17 years of uncertainty, the futuristic building is finally ready to tell its own story.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: South African engineering student built a three-bedroom house using soil and plastic waste; after success requests came in for more homes
articles.summary: Rest of World News: What if a house could be built from the very waste that usually ends up in landfills? That question became a reality for Matimba Mabonda, a South Afri.
articles.body: What if a house could be built from the very waste that usually ends up in landfills? That question became a reality for Matimba Mabonda, a South African chemical engineering graduate and MSc student at the University of Cape Town (UCT). Mabonda and his team have completed a three-bedroom house in Ennerdale, Johannesburg, using natural soil alongside plastic and other waste materials. The project was designed to explore whether sustainable construction could also provide a more affordable alternative to conventional brick-and-mortar homes. More than 90% of the home's walls were made from earth materials and plastic waste, according to UCT's Faculty of Engineering & the Built Environment. The house took less than a month to construct and, from the outside, looks much like the conventional homes around it. After the pilot was completed, the team began receiving requests from people interested in having similar houses built.From growing up in a shack to designing affordable homesFor Mabonda, the idea was deeply personal. He grew up in a shack in Grasmere, Ennerdale, Johannesburg, where he saw first-hand the difficulties associated with South Africa's housing shortage. After completing his chemical engineering degree at UCT, he joined his father, Ben, a contractor who had already built hundreds of homes. Together, they began exploring how construction could become more affordable and environmentally responsible. Mabonda had also established LolaGreen, a start-up focused on converting waste collected from landfills and the environment into durable building materials. His original idea involved “lolabricks”, made using plastic and industrial waste without cement or water. However, the machinery needed to manufacture them proved too expensive, prompting him to explore earth-building technologies instead.Soil and plastic waste became the building materialsThe pilot project eventually combined raw soil with plastic waste to create the materials used in the house. But turning ordinary earth into a suitable construction material was not as simple as digging it up and building with it. Mabonda explained that soil needs to be carefully analysed and tested to determine whether its composition is appropriate for construction. Different homes and locations can require different soil ratios, meaning the material has to be blended according to the desired building requirements. For the Ennerdale house, the team incorporated plastic waste into the raw soil while ensuring that the structure remained sound throughout construction. The finished property contains three bedrooms, a living area, kitchen, bathroom and garage, demonstrating that waste-based construction can extend beyond experimental walls or small structures.The three-bedroom house took less than a monthThe completed home looks surprisingly ordinary from the outside. That was partly the point. Rather than creating a structure that immediately announces itself as an experimental eco-project, Mabonda wanted to demonstrate that alternative construction materials could produce a comfortable home comparable to conventional housing. The three-bedroom house took less than a month to build and the family moved in after construction was completed. Mabonda said more than 90% of the walls were made from earth materials and plastic waste. He also described the house as naturally comfortable, remaining warm during winter and cool during summer, reducing the need for expensive air conditioning. The project therefore tackles several challenges simultaneously: construction cost, building time, waste management and the demand for housing.Success of the pilot brought requests for more housesThe first house was intended as a proof of concept, but its completion quickly created interest in scaling the idea. Mabonda said LolaGreen had already received a significant number of requests from people wanting houses constructed using waste materials. The appeal is not only environmental. According to Mabonda, the approach can be more cost-effective than traditional brick-and-mortar construction while also taking less time. His longer-term ambition is to help decarbonise the construction industry and demonstrate what can be achieved without relying entirely on conventional building materials. The next challenge is certification. Mabonda is in discussions with the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) as he works towards obtaining the necessary certification for the company's building approach.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2006, a couple paid $2.4 million for a Lake George lot once tied to a 42-room mansion; 20 years later, their 6,000-sq-ft compound with 300 feet of shoreline is asking $7.99 million
articles.summary: News News: On Lake George, where Adirondack mountains rise around some of New York's clearest waters, a property built around the boating lifestyle is now lookin.
articles.body: On Lake George, where Adirondack mountains rise around some of New York's clearest waters, a property built around the boating lifestyle is now looking for its next owner. The longtime Lake George compound belonging to George and Kathleen Badcock, owners of the historic Hacker-Craft motorboat brand, has been listed for $7.99 million, reports Mansion Global. The couple purchased the 1.37-acre property for $2.4 million in 2006, according to PropertyShark records, and transformed an empty lot into a substantial waterfront retreat. Two decades later, the property includes a roughly 6,000-square-foot home, 300 feet of shoreline and a three-bay boathouse. The property has an unusual history. The lot was once part of the grounds associated with a 42-room mansion, but when the Badcocks purchased it, the site was vacant. The couple, who had spent decades visiting Lake George, were drawn to its waterfront views and boating access. They built a residence designed to make the lake the centerpiece of daily life. The result is a five-bedroom home with four full bathrooms and two half baths, along with six fireplaces and multiple spaces designed for entertaining. Large expanses of glass bring views of the water into the main living areas, while expansive decks extend the home's living space outdoors.A house designed around the lakeThe great room serves as the central gathering space, featuring high ceilings and a stone fireplace. It connects with the dining area, wet bar and gourmet kitchen, creating an open entertaining area facing the lake. The first-floor primary suite includes its own fireplace, a spa-style bathroom and direct access to the waterfront. Additional features include an executive office, a lower-level family room with a fireplace, another wet bar, a screened lakeside porch and a guest suite, adds Mansion Global report. An attached three-car garage adds another unusual feature: living accommodations on the upper level, it adds.The rarest feature may be the boathouseFor owners whose lives revolve around boats, the property's three-bay boathouse could be its biggest attraction. The structure can accommodate boats up to 35 feet long and includes lifts and a sundeck. It currently houses three classic wooden boats belonging to the Badcocks: a 1925 Hacker-Craft and two Chris-Crafts dating to 1929 and 1954. The boathouse is particularly notable because similar construction would not be permitted under current regulations, making the existing structure a rare asset on Lake George.A showcase for the Hacker-Craft legacyThe property reflects the Badcocks' connection to classic boating. They acquired The Hacker Boat Co. in 2011, becoming owners of Hacker-Craft, a brand associated with handcrafted mahogany motorboats. Founded in Detroit in 1908 by John L. Hacker, the company later moved to New York state. During World War II, it also redesigned rescue boats for the Army Air Force. Hacker-Craft boats can require thousands of hours to complete and have appeared in campaigns for brands including Tommy Hilfiger, Nautica, Marks & Spencer and Tommy Bahama. The Badcocks' daughter, Erin, serves as the company's chief operating officer.Downsizing after decades on Lake GeorgeThe couple, both 77, are now preparing for a change. After spending roughly 42 years coming to Lake George, they plan to build or renovate a smaller home on the lake once the current property sells Their decision brings a rare Lake George offering to the market: a private waterfront compound combining extensive shoreline, a substantial residence and a historic-style boathouse. For prospective buyers, the $7.99 million property offers more than a luxury home. It is a carefully built retreat centered on one of the Adirondacks' defining attractions — life on the water.Images Courtesy: Mansion GlobalReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: A Fire Island glass house drew 350+ viewers at $5.25 million but no buyer; after $1.255 million in cuts, its $3.995 million ask is still nearly $1.3 million above Cherry Grove's record sale
articles.summary: News News: A striking glass house in Cherry Grove on New York’s Fire Island has attracted more than 350 viewers since it went on the market, but the attention ha.
articles.body: A striking glass house in Cherry Grove on New York’s Fire Island has attracted more than 350 viewers since it went on the market, but the attention has not yet resulted in a sale. The four-bedroom property, known as Crest House, was initially listed for $5.25 million in July 2026.The property has since undergone two major price reductions. According to Realtor, after first dropping to $4.85 million a few weeks after its launch, the asking price has now been cut to $3.995 million. That means the seller has reduced the price by a total of $1.255 million from the original listing.Even at the reduced price, the house would be far above the existing sales record in Cherry Grove if it sells close to its current asking price. According to listing agent Nikola (Niko) Cejic of Douglas Elliman’s Lord Chapin Team, the highest price ever paid for a property in Cherry Grove is $2.7 million.Despite the unusually high asking price, the property has generated considerable interest from potential buyers. Cejic said, “We have had over 350 people view the house,” Cejic says. “It got the most attention of any listing but wasn't selling.”Large oceanfront propertyCrest House sits on a rare 120-foot double lot and covers 7,130 square feet. The property is being sold fully furnished, giving the next owner a ready-to-use home.The house was custom-built in 2012 as a post-and-beam residence. It has 120 feet of direct ocean frontage and is fully solar-powered. Its design focuses heavily on the surrounding water, with the home positioned to make the most of its location.“The way the home was constructed, it was directed toward the water,” Cejic says. “And the thing that drew the owner here is its peace, calmness, and seclusion.”The three-storey home has several features designed to connect its interior with the outdoors. These include vaulted ceilings, a floating staircase, oversized windows and retractable glass walls. The property also has three fireplaces.Outside, there is nearly 5,000 square feet of living space. This includes large decks, a covered porch, a private courtyard and a heated pool. The outdoor areas were also designed with entertaining in mind.“It is a great house for large-scale entertaining,” Cejic says. “The seller wanted a modern sleek family home to entertain. They had a musician on the deck, and there was still a ton of space left. You could have a 200-person concert on the deck.”Why location mattersThe property’s setting is a major part of its appeal. Fire Island is a car-free community and can be reached from mainland Long Island by a short ferry ride. Within Cherry Grove, residents and visitors travel mainly on foot and along boardwalks.Cejic says this makes the community particularly secluded and contributes to its distinct character. “Cherry Grove is all walking and boardwalks, so it's very secluded,” Cejic says. “It's a real hidden gem and kept under the radar.”The listing agent also says the property is expected to serve as a second home for its eventual buyer because Fire Island is a resort town. The current marketing is aimed at buyers from Manhattan as well as members of the LGBTQ community.The house is also located close to Fire Island Pines. The community is about a 15-minute walk from Cherry Grove and has its own high-end property market. Fashion designer Michael Kors has listed a beachfront compound there for $6.25 million.For Crest House, however, the challenge remains finding a buyer willing to pay a price that would set a new record for Cherry Grove. “You can't get better than 120 feet of ocean frontage and beach access,” Cejic says. “It's just an incredible home.”Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: 'Significant moment' for chough reintroduction scheme in Kent
articles.summary: Eight wild-born red-billed chough chicks fledge, with sightings across east Kent.
articles.body:
Conservationists are celebrating the fledging of eight wild-born red-billed chough chicks in Kent.

The birds were born a year after the first wild chick to fledge since the species was reintroduced to the county in 2023 .

Eight captive-reared choughs were released in Dover that year, with the county's population now thought to be 35 and sightings reported in Thanet and Folkestone.

The fledgings were "a hugely significant moment" that showed species restoration work was "delivering real results", according to Kent Wildlife Trust's Paul Hadaway.

The group's director of conservation and engagement said: "This recovery reflects decades of habitat restoration, conservation grazing and partnership working to create landscapes where wildlife can thrive once again.

"Seeing the birds now spreading beyond Dover gives us real confidence they can continue to expand their range, strengthen the population and once again become an established part of Kent's landscape."

The birds disappeared from the county more than 200 years ago as a result of habitat loss but, according to conservationists, decades of restoration work enabled their return.

A further eight birds are expected to be released in Kent in September.

The reintroduction scheme is run by Kent Wildlife Trust with Paradise Park in Cornwall and Wildwood Trust.

Liz Corry, chough release supervisor at Wildwood Trust, said the project's success "fills me with immense pride".

"It is a true testament to the hard work and dedication of our staff, the partnership, and volunteers, not to mention the resilience of the birds themselves," she said.

New government-backed research will use DNA analysis to examine the diet of Kent's reintroduced choughs to inform habitat management.

articles.title: How significant are the Yemeni government’s military gains against Houthis?
articles.summary: Government forces make gains as fighting escalates, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.
articles.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised government says its forces have made significant gains against the Houthis as fighting has escalated in recent weeks, raising fears of a return to full-scale war.

The government forces on Saturday said they had recaptured strategically located territory in Hodeidah province under Houthi control and advanced in western Taiz.

However, the latest gains do not yet amount to a decisive shift in Yemen’s long-running war.

The Iran-aligned Houthis still control the capital, Sanaa, and several other cities, and have themselves recently advanced around Taiz as they seek to threaten the government-held port of al-Makha (Mocha) and move towards areas bordering the strategically vital Bab al-Mandeb strait, the chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Arabian Sea.

The fighting comes amid a wider regional conflict involving Saudi Arabia, which is a key backer of the Yemeni government.

Riyadh has carried out air strikes against positions recently captured by the Houthis, as the battle increasingly focuses on territory leading towards one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

What is the latest fighting on the ground?

The government forces have been fighting the Houthis across several fronts, with some of the heaviest clashes in Taiz and Hodeidah provinces, and along the western Red Sea coast.

The SABA news agency, controlled by Yemen’s internationally recognised government, reported on Saturday that the Yemeni military had taken control of Hais district in Hodeidah, citing an unidentified military source.

Hais is strategically located at the junction of Hodeidah, Taiz and Ibb provinces. The Houthis have yet to comment on this latest development.

The source also said government forces have regained areas around the al-Barh junction in western Taiz and advanced towards Houthi positions. Taiz is divided between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Fayad al-Numan, a Yemeni Information Ministry official, said government forces had also captured dozens of Houthi fighters during clashes in al-Jarahi district in southern Hodeidah.

Clashes in Taiz killed more than 60 people, including civilians, on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

On Thursday, fighting erupted as Houthi forces launched a major offensive along front lines in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah, using ballistic missiles, drones and artillery as ground forces attempted to advance towards government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that about 1,800 families have been displaced over the past two days as fighting escalated in Taiz.

Fighting renewed in early August after months of calm when Yemeni government forces launched attacks on Houthi positions across multiple front lines.

The Yemeni government re-established control over major southern and eastern territories following a Saudi-backed counteroffensive and the subsequent dissolution of the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC) in January.

They now aim to unite Yemen after bringing the areas under Houthi control under one administration.

But the Houthis have pushed towards government-held areas near al-Makha and territory bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait amid reinforcements and counteroffensives from the government forces.

The latest escalation follows a period of relative calm in Yemen that had largely held since a UN-brokered truce in April 2022. The ceasefire brought an end to major fighting since the Houthis’ capture of much of the country, including Sanaa, in 2014.

But Thursday’s attacks hint at a return to large-scale conflict.

The capture of Hais could be significant because of its position linking Hodeidah, Taiz and Ibb, while advances around al-Barh could help government forces push back against Houthi forces in western Taiz.

Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi said Yemen’s armed forces were capable of restoring control over the entire country and warned that Houthi “miscalculations” would lead to their “complete collapse”.

However, it is too early to describe the developments as a significant shift in control.

The Houthis had themselves seized positions near Taiz shortly before the government counteroffensive, according to an AFP news agency citing a military officer.

Houthi forces have also been attempting to cut off the government-held port of al-Makha, and advance towards areas bordering the Bab al-Mandeb strait.

The scale of government losses also shows how contested the battlefield remains. Twenty-six government soldiers were killed in several hours of fighting on Saturday alone, according to AFP’s military sources.

The escalation is also increasingly intertwined with the wider regional conflict linked to the US-Israel war on Iran.

The Iran-backed Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia in July and began targeting Saudi ships and territory, while Saudi Arabia has carried out air strikes against Houthi positions in Taiz.

Bab al-Mandeb has become particularly important after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. The Hormuz blockade has triggered a global energy crisis and is pushing the global economy into turbulence.

The waterway is a key transit route for Saudi oil, one of only two exit-entry points to the Red Sea, the other being the Suez Canal, raising the stakes as Houthi forces attempt to advance towards areas bordering the strait.

In July, Saudi Arabia announced a mission to form an international alliance to guard the Red Sea from attacks on shipping by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

articles.title: Mysterious settlement discovered after residents seemingly packed up and vanished
articles.summary: A medieval village near Halberstadt in Saxony-Anhalt was abandoned in a "highly orderly fashion," archaeologists say — but why the residents left remains a mystery.
articles.body: Archaeologists recently uncovered the remains of a medieval village that was mysteriously abandoned in Germany — raising questions about why its residents packed up and left. The excavation at the Am Frevelgraben site in Halberstadt, in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, revealed numerous traces of a medieval settlement, including parts of a multi-tiered ditch system. The State Office for Monument Preservation and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt announced the findings on Aug. 24. UNEXPECTED ANCIENT COMPLEX EMERGES NEAR BIBLICAL CITY LINKED TO JONAH AND ST PETER Archaeologists began excavating the site in March ahead of the development of a nearby industrial park, officials said. Historical maps suggest the settlement may be the remains of a medieval village known as Kühlingen. Archaeologists documented rows of pit houses, settlement pits and two wells at the site, while other traces suggest residents also made extensive use of the nearby riverbank. Overlapping features and houses built directly next to one another indicate the settlement developed in two phases, officials said — with its footprint shifting as new homes were constructed. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT Despite the well-preserved remains, however, archaeologists found surprisingly few artifacts — a detail officials found remarkable. "A few scattered ceramic shards and a handful of metal finds, including, for example, a bronze tap, fittings, and belt buckets, certainly represent only a fraction of the former possessions of the inhabitants," the release said. The settlement was abandoned "in a highly orderly fashion," Oliver Dietrich, a spokesperson for the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, told Fox News Digital. "It was indeed striking how few artifacts were left behind," he said. "Medieval deserted villages typically yield a wealth of artifacts." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Dietrich said archaeologists found no evidence of destruction or fire at the site, and said the reason behind the abandonment "remains a mystery at this time." "Further analysis will produce further insights into the abandonment process," he said. The settlement is "clearly medieval," though researchers are not sure precisely when it was abandoned, Dietrich added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Because of the scarcity of finds, radiocarbon analyses of selected animal bones are expected to provide a precise date," he said. As fascinating as it is, the expert added that Am Frevelgraben is one of hundreds of deserted medieval villages in Germany. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "The most drastic period of abandonment was during the 14th and 15th centuries," Dietrich said, citing the Black Death, migration and climate change. Often these villages "had too few resources to sustain the people," he said. The find follows a similar discovery made recently in neighboring Poland. articles.title: How Charlie Kirk inspired his mentor's fight to defend reality
articles.summary: Frank Turek stood feet away when Charlie Kirk was fatally shot at Utah Valley University. Now his new book carries on Kirk's apologetics mission.
articles.body: For decades, author Frank Turek has defended the idea that a Christian worldview offers the truest explanation of reality. The murder of his close friend, Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk one year ago, only reinforced that conviction. Now, Turek is sharing those beliefs in his new book, "The War on Reality: Recovering Truth in a World that Celebrates Lies," co-authored with Phoenix Hayes. The book argues that popular culture views about the family, gender, education and politics defy logic and aims to equip Christians to challenge these beliefs. Kirk's wife, Erika, wrote the foreword for the book, in which Turek says she reveals the source of her late husband's quiet confidence during hostile debates on college campuses. BENNY JOHNSON RECALLS HOW CHARLIE KIRK HELPED HIS FAMILY AFTER ARSON DESTROYED THEIR DC HOME "She writes that the reason Charlie would go to college campuses and not get flustered is because he knew that the foundation of his belief was true — that there is a God, he is not Him," Turek told Fox News Digital. "He has put us on this earth to know him and to make him known through Jesus," Turek said. "And everything else is really just details. And so he could stand firm on a college campus despite any kind of threat or despite any question that might come his way. But he knew he had to be prepared to answer those questions." As an example of this "war on reality," Turek pointed to the debate over transgender issues, which he argued has caused immeasurable harm to women and children. "It's a contradictory worldview that tragically is hurting children the most, because we have people now, politicians and mostly Democrats saying... what we ought to do is transition children that are confused about their sexuality," Turek said. "This is not care, this is child abuse. It's a war on women, by the way, because now women aren't protected in women's sports or in women's changing facilities." Turek mentored Kirk on applying strategies he discusses in the book, such as employing the laws of logic and identifying fallacies when responding to polarizing cultural topics. Their friendship began in 2020 after Kirk asked Turek to mentor him in Christian apologetics, which is the practice of defending Christianity with evidence and reasoning. Turek said their bond deepened over time until he came to view Kirk as a son. BILL MAHER TO APPEAR IN CHARLIE KIRK DOCUMENTARY, REMEMBERS LOVING HIS INTERVIEW WITH THE TPUSA LEADER "Charlie was the same person offstage that he was onstage. He was somebody that was always trying to learn," Turek told Fox News Digital. "It can be hard to mentor somebody smarter than you, but not with Charlie, because the only thing that exceeded his intellect was his humility. The few things that I knew that he wanted to know, he asked me to tell him. So we would get together and discuss questions he might get on a college campus, because I've been presenting on college campuses for about 20 years. And we would sharpen one another." Turek was standing just feet away when Kirk was shot and killed Sept. 10 at Utah Valley University during the first stop of TPUSA’s "The American Comeback Tour." At Kirk's memorial service weeks later, Turek reflected on his friend's faith. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "Now, I want you to know that Charlie, right now, is in heaven," Turek said at the service. "Not because he was a great husband and father, not because he saved millions of kids out of darkness on college campuses, not because he changed minds and chased votes to save the country, not because he sacrificed himself for his Savior. Charlie Kirk is in heaven because his Savior sacrificed himself for Charlie Kirk." Ultimately, Turek hopes his book encourages Christians and churches to speak out boldly in the public square and to carry on Kirk's legacy. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I hear from pastors all the time, 'I don't get involved in politics, I just preach the gospel,' to which I say to them, 'I guess you don't think the gospel is very important then.' And they say, 'Well, what do you mean?' And I say, 'Because the laws that are made politically can affect your ability to preach and live the gospel'... So for no other reason, Christians have to be involved in politics to protect our ability to preach and live the gospel, to have religious freedom," Turek said. "The second reason, major reason, is because we're called to love one another. And God set up governments to protect innocent people from evil. According to Romans 13, the government is supposed to punish wrongdoers. Why will we not put laws in place as Christians to punish people who are doing evil. We should," Turek said.

articles.title: Angry locals block famous beach as mass tourism protests escalate at vacation hot spot
articles.summary: Around 100 residents occupied Cala Saladeta beach in Ibiza to protest tourist overcrowding, demanding that locals reclaim the island's public spaces from visitors.
articles.body: Some 100 residents staged an occupation of a beach in Ibiza recently to protest overtourism amid growing frustration over mass tourism in Spain — and more action is apparently planned. The group gathered at Cala Saladeta, a popular tourist beach, last week, according to Balearic public broadcaster IB3. The protest was organized by the Ibiza Youth Association, a local youth group. INFLUENCERS REACHING PEAK BACKLASH AFTER SUMMER OF RUINED DESTINATIONS AND EXPERIENCES FOR AMERICANS Ibiza is one of Spain's Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea. The island is visited by many tourists, with its population swelling during the summer months. Known to locals as Eivissa, Ibiza received nearly 1.2 million tourists in the second quarter of 2025, according to data from the Balearic Islands Statistics Institute. Organizers rallied "against tourist overcrowding," IB3 reported, and activists handed out watermelon as part of a demand "that residents be able to enjoy the island's public spaces." CRUISE SHIP CRACKDOWN HITS TOURIST HOT SPOT AS CITY FAST-TRACKS NEW VISITOR TAX The group said in its manifesto that "our land and our culture are being directly pushed out of public spaces, and increasingly out of private spaces, as well, displayed solely as tourist attractions," according to local outlet CadeNA SER. The manifesto also decried a tourism model catering to "wealthy foreigners and famous partygoers," while arguing that housing, food and other living costs have become unaffordable for residents. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "[Young people are] fed up with not being able to enjoy [the island] as tourists do, because we believe we can no longer continue giving up spaces to the visitors brought by this extractive tourism model, which makes our lives in Ibiza more precarious," the manifesto added, per Cadena SER. The island's coves, which attract tourists during the busy summer season, were also a focus of the group's manifesto. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS The coves "should become our coves again, clean and peaceful," the manifesto said. "We want to reclaim places of tranquility." "We have decided that we want to reclaim places of tranquility, including during the summer," the statement added. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ In response to the recent protests, Ibiza Island Council President Vicent Marí said the island has been a "pioneer" in combating tourist overcrowding, according to Cadena SER. The Ibiza demonstration comes amid broader tensions surrounding mass tourism across Spain. In recent years, Barcelona residents have taken to the streets to protest mass tourism, with some demonstrators spraying visitors with water guns. articles.title: Body-worn cameras given to Sheffield school crossing wardens
articles.summary: Lollipop men and ladies in Sheffield will be given the cameras to combat aggressive behaviour.
articles.body:
Lollipop men and women in Sheffield have been given body-worn cameras in an effort to combat abuse and aggressive behaviour from drivers.

Sheffield City Council said school crossing wardens at several unspecified locations across the city would be given the cameras, which will record interactions, as part of a new initiative.

The local authority said the measure would create a safer environment for families walking to school in the new academic year and provide reassurance to staff working alone.

Wardens have been subjected to "unacceptable behaviour" and dangerous driving by a "small" number of motorists, the council added.

Jefferson Nwokeoma, the authority's assistant director of city transport said: "These body-worn cameras will help protect our staff, provide valuable evidence when incidents occur and encourage motorists to follow the rules of the road.

"Ultimately, this is about making the journey to school safer for everyone."

Drivers who fail to stop for a school crossing warden can be fined up to £1,000 and have three penalty points added to their licence.
