articles.title: Jaguar Land Rover may cut 4,000 jobs as Tata-owned carmaker targets £1.7bn savings and 300,000-vehicle break-even point a year after cyber attack, piling pressure on Andy Burnham’s ‘reindustrialise’ Britain pledge
articles.summary: UK News: Tata Motors-owned Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is opening a voluntary redundancy programme that could see around 4,000 jobs cut over the next two years, ac.
articles.body: Tata Motors-owned Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is opening a voluntary redundancy programme that could see around 4,000 jobs cut over the next two years, according to a UK media report. The development comes nearly a year after a cyber attack brought production at the British carmaker to a standstill for several weeks and as the company grapples with falling sales, rising costs and the impact of US tariffs.According to The Times, the luxury carmaker is expected to formally announce the redundancy programme on Monday. JLR, however, has already informed staff and trade union partners about the voluntary scheme, which will offer salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business.The company has said it needs to save approximately £1.7 billion over the next two years as it seeks to adapt to “evolving global market conditions”. It is also targeting a reduction in its break-even point to 300,000 vehicles.JLR targets £1.7bn in savingsA JLR spokesperson said the company had strengthened its “house of brands” and transformed its product portfolio over the past three years, but now needs to make further changes to improve efficiency.“Over the past three years, we have strengthened our house of brands and transformed our product portfolio for the next generation,” JLR said in a statement.“As we deliver the next phase of our strategy we must adapt to evolving global market conditions while targeting approximately £1.7 billion of savings over the next two years and reduce break-evens to 300,000 vehicles,” it said.“To achieve this, we must further simplify our organisation, improve efficiency and build greater resilience,” the company added.JLR said it had informed its employees and trade union partners about the voluntary redundancy programme and would provide further information to its colleagues first.Reports have suggested that around 4,000 employees could eventually lose their jobs, although JLR has not independently confirmed the figure.The company employs around 34,000 people across its three manufacturing sites in England and supports a further 120,000 British jobs through its supply chain.Announcement comes a year after major cyber attackThe proposed redundancies come almost exactly a year after JLR was hit by a major cyber attack that forced it to suspend manufacturing operations for several weeks.The disruption meant that the company was unable to produce vehicles during the shutdown and contributed to a 27% drop in production. The overall cost of the cyberattack was later estimated at around £1.9 billion.The incident has added to the pressures facing JLR as it attempts to recover from a difficult period for the global automotive industry.US President Donald Trump’s decision to impose a 10% tariff on UK car imports to one of JLR’s key markets has also affected the company’s global operations and sales.North America accounts for around 29% of JLR’s global sales, making the region particularly important to the luxury carmaker. The company is also facing growing competition from a new wave of more affordable Chinese car brands, which have put pressure on traditional manufacturers across global markets.PB Balaji under pressure as revenues fallJLR chief executive PB Balaji, previously Tata Motors’ finance chief, took charge at the carmaker last year amid mounting financial challenges.The company recorded a nearly 10% fall in revenue in its most recent quarter, to June 2026, adding to the pressure on Balaji to deliver savings across JLR’s luxury brands while navigating a difficult global market.The proposed workforce reduction is part of a wider effort to simplify the organisation, improve efficiency and reduce the number of vehicles the company needs to sell to break even.Unite warns workers should not pay the priceThe announcement has prompted a strong response from Unite, one of the UK’s major trade unions.Sharon Graham, general secretary of the Unite workers’ union, said there had been intensive discussions with the government over how to mitigate the potential job losses.“There have been intensive government discussions over the weekend to look at how to mitigate these job losses at JLR,” Graham said.“Once again, we will leave no stone unturned to support these workers. It cannot be acceptable that workers again are made to pay the price,” she added.Graham had earlier warned that a “perfect storm” of financial pressures had been hanging over the automotive industry for years.“Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments,” she said.“Years of under-investment, unsustainable zero-emission vehicle mandates and high industrial energy costs are crippling the industry. There must be further action.”The union is also expected to hold talks with Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds and JLR boss PB Balaji over the proposed workforce reductions.UK government responds to potential job lossesThe UK government has acknowledged the uncertainty facing JLR workers, their families and communities affected by the potential redundancies.A government spokesperson said, “We understand that this will be an uncertain and concerning time for affected workers, their families and wider communities.”The government also pointed to measures it has taken to support the UK automotive industry, including efforts to reduce electricity costs for manufacturers, £4 billion in capital and R&D funding for zero-emission vehicle manufacturing and a £2 billion electric car grant aimed at encouraging consumers to buy EVs.Andy Burnham’s ‘reindustrialise’ pledge faces fresh pressureThe developments are likely to add to the pressure on Andy Burnham, who recently pledged to “reindustrialise” Britain after becoming Prime Minister.JLR remains a major employer and supports tens of thousands of additional jobs through its supply chain, making any large-scale workforce reduction significant for the UK’s manufacturing sector.The proposed redundancies also highlight the challenges facing the government as it attempts to strengthen domestic manufacturing while British carmakers contend with high operating costs, weaker demand, international tariffs, the transition to electric vehicles and intensifying competition from Chinese manufacturers.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: What the US militarisation of Latin America could look like
articles.summary: More US military involvement and larger regional defence budgets mean less social spending and worse democracy outcomes.
articles.body:
Latin America is seeing growing military activity by the United States. Under the umbrella of the Americas Counter-Cartel Coalition (ACCC), launched by President Donald Trump in March, US forces are carrying out strikes on vessels suspected of drug trafficking, while US officials are deepening ties and cooperation with Latin American militaries.

This reflects the growing push from Washington towards militarisation of the region, as left-wing politics decline. For Latin America, this may spell the return of coercive US policies.

The projection of US military power, whether through coordinated operations, US boots on the ground or the use of regional bases, will not help improve regional security and fight crime. If anything, it could undermine democracy and usher in more violence and instability.

Apart from the US, the ACCC includes 17 Latin American and Caribbean nations: Argentina, Bahamas, Belize, Bolivia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Guyana, Guatemala, Paraguay, Jamaica, Panama, Trinidad and Tobago, Honduras, El Salvador, the Dominican Republic, Colombia and Peru.

Although Venezuela is not officially part of the coalition, it appears it has opened up its territory for US operations. With its informal participation, the ACCC is able to complete the “Andean arc”, which accounts for the entirety of the cocaine production distributed and sold in the US and Europe. This is also where many of the region’s organised crime groups operate.

But the coalition appears to be about more than just narcotics. Trump has said that the ACCC’s mandate is to counter “malign foreign influences from outside the Western Hemisphere” – a veiled reference to China.

The fact that the ACCC was created in Florida just two months after the US army had carried out a ground operation in Venezuela and deposed its president, Nicolas Maduro, was also significant.

Another step in that direction came on August 4 , when the US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) announced the creation of the Western Hemisphere Joint Task Force, which will “synchronise U.S. military operations with allies and partners to counter threats, strengthen regional security and respond rapidly to crises across the Western Hemisphere”. The new task force will integrate command and control of the 18 members of the ACCC.

Washington is clearly seeking to reassert coercive hegemony over the region. It wants to exert greater influence and control over security and defence decisions in the region, in what appears to be a resurrection of the 1823 Monroe Doctrine, now renamed the Trump Corollary.

Recent operations in the region have shed light on what a renewed US force projection might look like. In June, Trump revealed on Truth Social that the US army, acting in coordination with Venezuelan authorities, carried out an air strike targeting Hector Guerrero Flores, leader of the criminal gang, Tren de Aragua, in Bolivar state. In a statement, the Venezuelan government later acknowledged the joint action by both countries.

In late August and early September, the newly created Western Hemisphere Joint Task Force attacked several suspected vessels, killing at least two people. This was a continuation of the “Southern Spear” operation, which to date has killed at least 220 people with no investigation launched into whether they were all indeed involved in drug trafficking.

Added to this is the announcement made by Secretary of Defence, Pete Hegseth, that newly inaugurated Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has authorised the US to conduct military operations in Colombia “to combat narco-terrorism”.

All of this means, the US is seeking greater military reach in Latin America, whether in the form of bilateral cooperation through joint operations or unilateral action involving overflights of the countries’ territories and even access to national military bases. There will likely be US troops on the ground involved in operations to neutralise whatever activities the US perceives as a threat.

Latin America is not new to US military intervention. During the Cold War, Washington was extensively involved in mostly covert activity in the region, but there were also overt operations, such as the invasion of the Bay of Pigs in Cuba and of the island nation of Grenada. In many cases, the civilian population faced violence as a result of the US interventions.

After the Cold War, US involvement took the shape of anti-drug campaigns, which similarly did not produce positive outcomes for local communities. Take the example of Plan Colombia (2000-2015), which was meant to combat drug trafficking and leftist insurgent groups.

Although it contributed to the weakening of insurgent organisations, it also produced a lot of violence, including by the US-trained Colombian military, which was accused of killing thousands of civilians and claiming they were rebels to “show results”. US troops stationed in Colombia as part of training programmes were also accused of raping dozens of Colombian women and girls and smuggling drugs and weapons.

Plan Colombia, which received $10bn in US funding, ended up militarising Colombia’s security agenda, intensifying armed conflicts and cartel violence, as well as the persecution of union leaders, peasants and the civilian population. It failed to stop the proliferation of coca plantations.

Given the past historical record, the US push for the militarisation of Latin American states and a greater military presence in the region is unlikely to bring more security.

The effect of greater US military engagement in the region will not be limited to the security sector only.

Washington has made clear that membership in the ACCC should translate into greater national spending on defence. That means national budgets will be thrown out of balance and resources will be diverted away from vital sectors such as education, health care, housing and social security. Worsening social services provision will likely lead to more public discontent.

Then there is the question of sovereignty. The US will seek to influence the design of security and defence policies—particularly with regard to maintaining internal security and the scope of military cooperation. Washington can and will put pressure on governments and legislatures to align with its agenda.

The fact that US officials have insisted that ACCC member countries withdraw from the International Criminal Court does not bode well for transparency and accountability. Clearly, the aim is to ensure impunity for US armed forces and their allies.

It is highly likely that a lack of transparency and accountability will exacerbate the authoritarian trend that has been emerging in Latin American politics, with well-known consequences: weakening of institutions, increased discretionary power, the erosion of the rule of law, and, consequently, a decline in citizens’ quality of life.

For the Trump administration, the ACCC may be an important foreign policy win. But for Latin American societies, it is yet another threat to their fragile democratic institutions.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Honeytrap, Rs 1 crore demand, 3 arrests: Cops probe UP officer’s 'blackmail' before suicide
articles.summary: BASTI: A 56-year-old police station officer in Basti allegedly died by suicide after being trapped in a honeytrap and subjected to blackmail, with pol.
articles.body: BASTI: A 56-year-old police station officer in Basti allegedly died by suicide after being trapped in a honeytrap and subjected to blackmail, with police claiming that a woman and her associates had demanded Rs 1 crore from him.Police on Sunday arrested the woman, her father and a lawyer in connection with the case and sent all three to judicial custody.The deceased, Suryaprakash Singh, was the station officer of Walterganj police station. Originally from Bhilampur Chhapra village in Azamgarh, Singh had about four years left before retirement. He is survived by his wife, a son and two daughters.Singh had been transferred to Basti from Siddharthnagar and was initially posted to the police lines. He took charge as Walterganj SO on April 18, 2026.On August 29, Singh was found hanging at his government accommodation near the district collectorate.Before his death, he had reportedly posted a WhatsApp status on his personal mobile number that read: “Wealth and property are necessary, but nothing is greater than peace and love.”According to DIG Sanjeev Tyagi, police arrested Priyanka Chaudhary, 32, her father Ramnayan Chaudhary, and lawyer Vijay Prakash from outside Sadar Hospital on Sunday.Police said the arrests followed questioning of Singh's family members, surveillance and analysis of call detail records (CDRs), which indicated that Singh had been in contact with the three accused.Investigators claim that Vijay Prakash was involved in collecting the money allegedly extorted through blackmail. Police have recovered a Bolero vehicle and three mobile phones from the accused.Police said Priyanka, a resident of Gandhar in the Walterganj area, had been living separately from her husband for around 10 years. She had reportedly worked at beauty parlours and spa centres in Mumbai.According to investigators, Priyanka allegedly developed relationships with financially well-off men and subsequently recorded their audio, video calls and private conversations.She would then allegedly use the material to threaten and blackmail them for money.Police further claimed that she used WhatsApp chats and video calls to maintain contact with her targets.Investigators said Priyanka would at times allegedly threaten or intimidate victims by making video calls showing herself apparently cutting her wrist, creating fear that she might harm herself if her demands were not met.According to police, her father Ramnayan and lawyer Vijay Prakash allegedly assisted her in collecting the money. Investigators suspect that the proceeds of the alleged extortion were shared among the three.During the investigation, police reportedly found that the accused had allegedly collected around Rs 24 lakh from three other individuals. One of the reported victims is a doctor.Police suspect that Singh was another target of the alleged extortion network and are now investigating whether additional people were targeted or blackmailed by the accused.Police said Priyanka lived within the jurisdiction of Walterganj police station and had approached Singh in connection with a case she had filed against her husband.During their interactions over the case, the two reportedly became acquainted and subsequently developed a close relationship. Police allege that Priyanka later began blackmailing Singh.Investigators said that on August 29, the day Singh died, lawyer Vijay Prakash spoke to him over the phone at around 1:41 pm and allegedly demanded Rs 1 crore.According to the police version, Singh was unable to arrange the demanded amount and died by suicide before making the payment.The investigation is continuing to establish the complete sequence of events, the alleged financial transactions and the involvement of the three accused in the suspected blackmail operation.Singh's son Sandeep Singh has demanded strict punishment for those responsible for his father's death.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: US envoys in Kyiv, but Russian strikes persist across Ukraine: 8 killed, 69 injured
articles.summary: International News: Russia’s aerial campaign across Ukraine continued as Moscow and Kyiv observed a temporary pause on airstrikes against each other’s capitals, with at l.
articles.body: Russia’s aerial campaign across Ukraine continued as Moscow and Kyiv observed a temporary pause on airstrikes against each other’s capitals, with at least eight people killed and 69 injured in Russian attacks over the past day, according to Ukrainian authorities cited by The Kyiv Independent.The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched 108 drones overnight, of which Ukrainian air defences intercepted 82, along with six S8000 Banderol missiles. Russian missiles and drones struck 11 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at seven locations, according to the report.The latest attacks came as the US stepped up diplomatic efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war, with President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arriving in Kyiv on September 6 for talks with Ukrainian officials.The two envoys arrived a day after holding more than three hours of discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. The meeting did not produce an immediate breakthrough, although a White House official said the talks covered “substantive plans for next steps” that would be announced in the coming weeks.Capital strikes paused amid US diplomacyThe temporary arrangement covers aerial attacks against Moscow and Kyiv but does not amount to a broader ceasefire.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on September 5 that Russian forces would not strike Kyiv for three days beginning at midnight. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was prepared to refrain from attacking Moscow through the end of September 7.Ukraine had proposed a wider three-day halt covering fighting along the front line as well, but Putin said Russia had not agreed to the proposal.Russian forces nevertheless continued attacks elsewhere in Ukraine.Officials reported no overnight strikes on Kyiv city, although Kyiv Oblast came under attack as Russian missiles and drones targeted other parts of the country.Trump envoys arrive in KyivWitkoff and Kushner’s visit to Kyiv comes as Washington seeks to build on its renewed diplomatic push following their meeting with Putin.A White House official described the Moscow discussions as focused on “substantive plans for next steps”. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks substantive, constructive and extremely frank.Putin said Russia expected to achieve its objectives and maintained that the “root causes” of the war needed to be addressed.The Moscow talks therefore failed to produce an immediate agreement, but Washington has signalled that discussions on possible next steps will continue.Zelenskyy seeks security guaranteesAhead of the meeting with the US envoys, Zelenskyy convened Ukraine’s negotiating team and said Kyiv was prepared for a substantive and realistic discussion.He said Ukraine wanted to end the war but also needed security guarantees and a dignified post-war peace.Zelenskyy added that Ukraine had prepared its proposals for the talks.The continued Russian strikes underline the limits of the temporary capital arrangement, with fighting and aerial attacks continuing across other parts of Ukraine even as Washington attempts to broker a wider settlement.

articles.title: Bosnian Serbs strengthen ties with Israel amid tensions
articles.summary: Opening of Israeli commerce office deepens ties between Republika Srpska and Israel.
articles.body:
The Israeli Chamber of Commerce last week opened an office in Banja Luka, the seat of government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina entity of Republika Srpska, in a move officials said would “further strengthen” the two sides’ ties.

The opening comes when Israel faces growing international criticism due to its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, including by the Sarajevo-based Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the other main political entity within Bosnia.

But in Republika Srpska, Israel has enjoyed strong support since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023. Milorad Dodik, the entity’s former president and effective leader, has frequently expressed pro-Israeli views positioning Republika Srpska as a key ally of Israel in the Balkans.

Following the outbreak of the Gaza war, Dodik said that Republika Srpska fully supports Israel’s right to self-defence, while the Palace of the Republic in Banja Luka was illuminated with the colours of the Israeli flag.

Dodik, who last year was stripped of his post and banned from holding political office for six years. That was after being convicted for refusing to comply with the decisions by the international envoy overseeing the peace deal that ended Bosnia’s 1990s war. He has opposed initiatives for the international recognition of Palestine. In August 2025, he said “a state that does not exist in reality cannot be lawfully recognised”.

Speaking at the opening ceremony in Banja Luka on Thursday, Dodik highlighted the political and historical ties between the Serb and Jewish people and what he described as their similar “suffering”.

“We have shown that we can, under impossible conditions and in an environment that is historically speaking hostile, preserve our identity and our holy word, which is freedom,” said Dodik.

Israel’s Ambassador in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Galit Peleg, said the office in Banja Luka is aimed at connecting businesses and to promote “investment cooperation“ between the two sides, without offering details.

“At a time of protests and threats in Sarajevo, the Office of President Milorad Dodik offered us a beautiful building in Banja Luka,” Geleg said at the ceremony, referring to the pro-Palestine demonstrations in Bosnia during the war on Gaza.

Dodik said Republika Srpska will create a support programme for new technologies from Israel, without disclosing details. Similarly, Republika Srpska authorities have touted the possibility of a significant Israeli investment, without providing any information.

The office’s president is Amir Gross Kabiri, an Israeli businessman, industrialist and investor who in recent years has become one of the most prominent figures in Bosnia’s economic and political life. He became known to the country’s wider public after his company, a subsidiary of the M.T. Abraham Group, an international conglomerate and investment group, signed a contract in 2020 to lease the facilities of the collapsed Mostar aluminium giant Aluminij.

After signing the agreement on the office opening, Ana Trisic Babic, the acting director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republic of Srpska, said the entity and Israel “have long nurtured friendly relations”, which she linked to “the historical experiences of the two peoples and the challenges they face”.

She added that the authorities of Republic of Srpska view Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s support for the opening of the office as a confirmation of those relations.

Davor Gjenero, a Zagreb-based analyst with extensive knowledge of political affairs in the Western Balkans, said the office opening will give Republika Srpska’s authorities an opportunity to alleviate the entity’s significant financial problems, including rising debt.

He said Republika Srpska “is facing a kind of bankruptcy and any kind of economic activity with Israel can be also part” of its strategy to address the issue.

Gjenero also highlighted the “connection” between the policies of Dodik and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, which he described as a potentially “dangerous” development amid rising tensions in Bosnia.

“This could also be a sign that centrifugal processes are taking place, which could pose a serious threat to the unity and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina,” he said.

Gjenero argued that the cooperation between the Republika Srpska and Israel, along with the growing cooperation between Serbia and Israel – particularly in the military sector – could further increase tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

He said “any activity” by the Republic of Srpska “without coordination with Sarajevo can be a serious problem for Bosnia and Herzegovina in its dialogue with the European Union”, as the country seeks EU membership.

“Also, any kind of making Dodik stronger is dangerous for relations between Sarajevo and Banja Luka and internal relations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.”

articles.title: Bosnian Serbs strengthen ties with Israel amid tensions
articles.summary: Opening of Israeli commerce office deepens ties between Republika Srpska and Israel.
articles.body:
The Israeli Chamber of Commerce recently opened an office in Banja Luka, Republika Srpska, to strengthen ties with the region, which has shown strong support for Israel during the Gaza war.

Milorad Dodik, former leader of Republika Srpska, has expressed pro-Israeli views and highlighted historical ties between Serb and Jewish people, positioning the entity as a key ally of Israel in the Balkans.

The office's opening is seen as an opportunity for Republika Srpska to address significant financial problems, but analysts warn that increased cooperation with Israel could escalate tensions in Bosnia and pose a threat to the country's unity and sovereignty.

The Israeli Chamber of Commerce last week opened an office in Banja Luka, the seat of government of the Bosnia and Herzegovina entity of Republika Srpska, in a move officials said would "further strengthen" the two sides' ties.

The opening comes when Israel faces growing international criticism due to its genocidal war against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, including by the Sarajevo-based Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the other main political entity within Bosnia.

But in Republika Srpska, Israel has enjoyed strong support since the start of the war on Gaza in October 2023. Milorad Dodik, the entity's former president and effective leader, has frequently expressed pro-Israeli views positioning Republika Srpska as a key ally of Israel in the Balkans.

Following the outbreak of the Gaza war, Dodik said that Republika Srpska fully supports Israel's right to self-defence, while the Palace of the Republic in Banja Luka was illuminated with the colours of the Israeli flag.

Dodik, who last year was stripped of his post and banned from holding political office for six years. That was after being convicted for refusing to comply with the decisions by the international envoy overseeing the peace deal that ended Bosnia's 1990s war. He has opposed initiatives for the international recognition of Palestine. In August 2025, he said "a state that does not exist in reality cannot be lawfully recognised".

Speaking at the opening ceremony in Banja Luka on Thursday, Dodik highlighted the political and historical ties between the Serb and Jewish people and what he described as their similar "suffering".

"We have shown that we can, under impossible conditions and in an environment that is historically speaking hostile, preserve our identity and our holy word, which is freedom," said Dodik.

Israel's Ambassador in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Galit Peleg, said the office in Banja Luka is aimed at connecting businesses and to promote "investment cooperation" between the two sides, without offering details.

"At a time of protests and threats in Sarajevo, the Office of President Milorad Dodik offered us a beautiful building in Banja Luka," Geleg said at the ceremony, referring to the pro-Palestine demonstrations in Bosnia during the war on Gaza.

Dodik said Republika Srpska will create a support programme for new technologies from Israel, without disclosing details. Similarly, Republika Srpska authorities have touted the possibility of a significant Israeli investment, without providing any information.

The office's president is Amir Gross Kabiri, an Israeli businessman, industrialist and investor who in recent years has become one of the most prominent figures in Bosnia's economic and political life. He became known to the country's wider public after his company, a subsidiary of the M.T. Abraham Group, an international conglomerate and investment group, signed a contract in 2020 to lease the facilities of the collapsed Mostar aluminium giant Aluminij.

After signing the agreement on the office opening, Ana Trisic Babic, the acting director of the Office for International Cooperation of the Republic of Srpska, said the entity and Israel "have long nurtured friendly relations", which she linked to "the historical experiences of the two peoples and the challenges they face".

She added that the authorities of Republic of Srpska view Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's support for the opening of the office as a confirmation of those relations.

Davor Gjenero, a Zagreb-based analyst with extensive knowledge of political affairs in the Western Balkans, said the office opening will give Republika Srpska's authorities an opportunity to alleviate the entity's significant financial problems, including rising debt.

He said Republika Srpska "is facing a kind of bankruptcy and any kind of economic activity with Israel can be also part" of its strategy to address the issue.

Gjenero also highlighted the "connection" between the policies of Dodik and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic, which he described as a potentially "dangerous" development amid rising tensions in Bosnia.

"This could also be a sign that centrifugal processes are taking place, which could pose a serious threat to the unity and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina," he said.

Gjenero argued that the cooperation between the Republika Srpska and Israel, along with the growing cooperation between Serbia and Israel – particularly in the military sector – could further increase tensions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

He said "any activity" by the Republic of Srpska "without coordination with Sarajevo can be a serious problem for Bosnia and Herzegovina in its dialogue with the European Union", as the country seeks EU membership.

"Also, any kind of making Dodik stronger is dangerous for relations between Sarajevo and Banja Luka and internal relations in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

articles.title: Isro will remain ‘bedrock of Indian space sector’, says Goenka
articles.summary: India News: BENGALURU: Two days after employee associations representing thousands of Isro staff sought a formal written clarification on Isro’s future, Pawan Goe.
articles.body: BENGALURU: Two days after employee associations representing thousands of Isro staff sought a formal written clarification on Isro’s future, Pawan Goenka, chairman, Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe) said that Isro will remain the “bedrock of the Indian space sector”.“...Let me say it unequivocally: Isro’s role is by no means diminishing. It will remain the bedrock of the Indian space sector. The reforms since 2020 are about expanding India’s overall space ecosystem. IN-SPACe will facilitate and authorise greater non-govt participation, while NSIL will help commercialise mature capabilities,” he said in a statement.His statement about Space PSU NSIL helping commercialisation of mature capabilities comes at a time when IN-SPACe has been announcing Expressions of Interest (EoIs) and plans to transfer technology to the private sector.In fact, IN-SPACe had even announced an EoI inviting private industry to operate the proposed second spaceport in Kulasekarapattinam in Tamil Nadu, once it has been developed by Isro and the Department of Space.The joint representation by Isro employees had pointed to a recent public statement made by Goenka on Isro eventually “not manufacturing any launch vehicles”, they asked if his statement “represents an approved decision of the Govt of India, Space Commission or DoS… If approved, the date, authority and text of the policy decision may kindly be indicated.”“The idea is to let industry increasingly manufacture and scale mature launch vehicles, satellites and other systems, while Isro focuses on what it is uniquely placed to do: advanced R&D, scientific missions, strategic missions, new technologies, and infrastructure that is too complex for the private sector to develop on its own,” Goenaka said.He said Isro will remain at the core of India’s space programme leading frontier research and the next generation of national missions, including the Bharatiya Antariksh Station by 2035, an Indian crewed mission to the Moon by 2040, next-generation launch systems, and sustained lunar and planetary exploration.“The direction is not a smaller Isro. It is a larger Indian space ecosystem, with Isro pushing the technological frontier,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A US war veteran named her Memphis home ‘Serenity’ after 11 quiet years; Elon Musk’s largest US AI data centre moved next door and she says her power bill doubled
articles.summary: US News: After serving in the US military during the Gulf War, veteran Loretta Thornton settled in a wooded home in Memphis, Tennessee. Living with post-trauma.
articles.body: After serving in the US military during the Gulf War, veteran Loretta Thornton settled in a wooded home in Memphis, Tennessee. Living with post-traumatic stress disorder, she named her house 'Serenity' and spent 11 peaceful years there. That peace ended when Elon Musk's technology company, xAI, built a huge computing facility in an abandoned warehouse next door. The site, known as Colossus II, is now the largest operating data centre in the United States. Thornton says the constant noise and fumes have badly affected her quality of life, while rising local power demand has doubled her electricity bill. "When they cranked this up, I thought I was back in Desert Storm," Thornton said. "I thought I was stuck back in the middle of a war. That's what it sounds like to me." In reporting for Australia's ABC News, journalist Bradley McLennan documented how the industrial site operates around the clock. Thornton describes a constant sound similar to jet engines and fumes from gas turbines that burn her eyes and throat. "I feel stomach-fold-up-sucker-punched, because I never thought anything like this would move in in my life," she said.Local backlash meets national political tensionThe rapid expansion in Memphis reflects a wider US trend in which data centres are being built faster than local governments can update their rules. With the American midterm elections approaching, the issue has become a major political flashpoint. President Donald Trump remains a strong supporter of data centre investment, warning that towns that reject them risk becoming "backward and poor". Speaking to cryptocurrency leaders at the White House, Trump urged local authorities to welcome the projects. "If I were the mayor of a town or the governor of a state and I had a chance to get a big plant in, an AI plant or a data centre, I would absolutely want it because the jobs are enormous … and the taxes paid are enormous," Trump said. However, several Republican candidates are breaking with the White House and siding with unhappy residents. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott issued a moratorium on new data centres. In Wisconsin, candidate Tom Tiffany called his opponent "Data Centre David Crowley". A Republican Senate campaign memo from Ohio, reported by Axios, described the facilities as an anchor around candidate Jon Husted's neck, warning that political losses over the issue could have nationwide effects. An August poll by YouGov found that only 24 per cent of Americans believe building new data centres is good for the country. More than 200 US jurisdictions have imposed moratoriums to slow new projects, while Memphis city councillors are considering a similar freeze.Fumes, noise and disputed water suppliesAlong the Tennessee-Mississippi border, xAI operates or is building at least four large data centres. Residents say weak regulations allowed the facilities to begin operating without public notice or votes by the city council. Amber Sherman, who lives near xAI's Colossus I site, blames the facility for a respiratory illness. "Elon Musk has been here exploiting Memphis on purpose because there are no guardrails in place," Sherman said. "I think that he sees Memphis as a sacrifice zone like a lot of people do. They see us as the path of least resistance and don't think that Memphians are going to fight back."KeShaun Pearson, who represents Memphis Community Against Pollution, told ABC News that technology companies are taking advantage of outdated zoning rules. "xAI and Elon Musk aren't the first perpetrators, they are just the newest ones, and they are moving at a velocity we have never seen," Pearson said. Water use has also caused anger. In 2024, Musk promised to build an 80 million US dollar water recycling facility that would provide 10 million gallons of grey water each day for cooling, reducing pressure on the regional aquifer. Two years later, construction remains largely stalled, with xAI moving the expected restart date to January 2027. Sarah Houston of the advocacy group Protect Our Aquifer said freedom of information requests showed that one xAI data centre uses at least 800,000 gallons of clean drinking water every day. "Until then it is a lot of words and a lot of empty promises," Houston said about the delayed recycling plant.Legal battles and reluctant acceptanceEnvironmental groups and local residents are taking legal action. The Southern Environmental Law Center filed a lawsuit claiming xAI installed dozens of gas turbines without permits. The turbines allegedly release smog-forming pollution, soot and formaldehyde. The City of Memphis carried out independent air tests near xAI facilities and found no dangerous levels of pollutants. However, separate class-action lawsuits over noise pollution are continuing. Mississippi resident Taylor Logsdon joined a class-action lawsuit over the noise, despite facing criticism from neighbours. "A lot of these people here, they've told us all, 'Why don't you just move?'" Logsdon said. "I can't move. I'm a stay-at-home mum and my husband doesn't make that much money. We bought the house at like $70,000 you can't find that no more, there's no way." Business groups such as the Greater Memphis Chamber argue that city leaders should negotiate for stronger economic benefits instead of banning the projects. They say tens of millions of dollars in property taxes are important for a city where a quarter of the population lives in poverty. For Thornton, taking on one of the world's richest people feels almost impossible. "If you start fighting with him, don't you know you'll be dead before it's settled?" Thornton said. "Maybe I can help somebody else by speaking out but I know it's not going anywhere. They're not going to shut that down."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Witkoff, Kushner reach Kyiv after meeting Putin as Washington steps up Ukraine peace push
articles.summary: Europe News: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reached Kyiv on Sunday for their first official visit to Ukraine, as Washington renewed efforts to f.
articles.body: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reached Kyiv on Sunday for their first official visit to Ukraine, as Washington renewed efforts to find a way to end the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion more than four years ago.The visit came a day after the two American representatives held more than three hours of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Their trip to Kyiv is part of a renewed diplomatic effort by the Trump administration, even as Russia and Ukraine continue to launch attacks against each other.US efforts to broker an end to the conflict had slowed in recent months, with the Trump administration turning much of its attention towards the war involving Iran.The situation on the battlefield remains difficult. Russia has increasingly used fast-moving, jet-powered drones in its attacks, while Ukrainian forces continue to face Russian troops along a front line stretching about 1,250 kilometres.Zelenskyy says Ukraine is ready for talksUkrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv was prepared to hold a serious discussion with Witkoff and Kushner.“We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed. A just and sustainable postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are prepared,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.The two US envoys travelled to Kyiv by train and were received by senior Ukrainian officials at the railway station. They later met Zelenskyy during a ceremony at St Sophia Square.Kyrylo Budanov, Zelenskyy's chief of staff, said representatives from Ukraine's European partners, including France, Germany and the United Kingdom, were also present in Kyiv.Moscow meeting ends without major breakthroughWitkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday, but neither side announced a major breakthrough after the closed-door discussions.Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov called the talks constructive, frank and useful, but did not reveal any specific agreement or progress.According to Ushakov, Russia presented its “comprehensive assessment” of the military situation in Ukraine. However, the discussions also covered issues beyond the war.“Economic issues and potentially large, mutually beneficial joint projects for Russia and America were discussed in considerable detail,” he said.Witkoff and Kushner, who is US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, had last visited Moscow in January, when they also met Putin at the Kremlin.Fighting continues despite diplomatic effortsThe diplomatic activity has taken place against the backdrop of continued attacks by both sides.Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to pause attacks on each other's capitals during the talks. However, officials reported exchanges of fire overnight into Sunday.Ukraine's State Emergency Service said Russian attacks in several regions killed one person and injured at least 10 others.A Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia killed a 74-year-old man and wounded three others. Another drone strike damaged an apartment building in the Khmelnytskyi region and injured seven people.Ukraine's air force said it had intercepted 82 of the 108 drones launched by Russia overnight, along with six missiles.Russian authorities also reported a Ukrainian drone attack. A man was killed and a woman seriously injured after a drone struck a vehicle in Russia's Belgorod border region.Russia's Defence Ministry said its air defences had destroyed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight across 14 Russian regions, Crimea and the waters of the Black and Azov seas.Ukrainians remain divided over peace prospectsThe renewed diplomatic activity has brought some hope in Ukraine, although many remain doubtful that it will lead to an immediate end to the fighting.In Kyiv, dozens of people gathered for the daily 9 am moment of silence held across the country to remember Ukrainian soldiers who have died in the war.Among them was 67-year-old Nataliia Lipei, whose son Viktor was killed in December 2022. Despite health problems, she has travelled to different cities to take part in the commemorations. She said she hoped the latest meetings would finally help end the conflict.“I hope these steps and these meetings will definitely produce results, because there has been so much bloodshed and so many deaths here that we have to stop all of this,” Lipei told The Associated Press.Others were far less optimistic. Oleksandr Pastukhov, a 27-year-old video editor who attended the commemoration, said previous diplomatic efforts had failed to produce lasting results.“We’ve already seen delegations like this come here before,” he said. “We’ve seen this so-called ceasefire for three days, which ended after just a couple of hours, and now we’re supposed to naively think that two people will come and change something.”Pope Leo XIV also renewed his call for peace in Ukraine during his Sunday prayer at the Vatican. He said he hoped the latest diplomatic efforts would lead to meaningful progress.“I hope that the efforts undertaken in recent days to resume negotiations will bear concrete fruit and make way for diplomacy," he told the gathered faithful in St. Peter’s Square at the Vatican.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Jamaican officials to bring reparations petition to King Charles
articles.summary: The King will be asked to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
articles.body:
The Jamaican government will hand a petition to King Charles over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said.

It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica.

Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured".

She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era.

'Ghana was the crime scene': The country leading the demand for slavery reparations

African and Caribbean nations call for formal apology for transatlantic slavery

The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Court are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress.

The petition is not a demand for payment.

Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined."

Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General to ensure the petition is correctly lodged.

A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today."

When slavery was abolished across most of the empire in 1833, the British government paid £20 million to slave owners in compensation. The loans taken out to raise the money were paid off in 2015.

Grange said: "Up to 2015, Britain was paying the slave masters, because we were being considered property.

"The question really should be: if in modern times we're still paying back the slave masters for the property that was our people, our ancestors, for property that was because of the abolition of slavery, then why shouldn't we be pursuing some remedy at this time?"

Grange will also meet with British Museum officials to "advance discussions on the repatriation of artefacts" taken from Jamaica during the colonial era.

She said: "They are priceless, they are significant to the story of Jamaica and we are working to bring them home."

In 2015, David Cameron, who was prime minister at the time, ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade, while visiting Jamaica.

Speaking to MPs in Jamaica's parliament, Cameron said slavery was "abhorrent in all its forms". He added that he hoped they could "move on from this painful legacy and continue to build for the future".
